top_cited_works.title: CRIMSON: An open-source software framework for cardiovascular integrated modelling and simulation
top_cited_works.abstract: In this work, we describe the CRIMSON (CardiovasculaR Integrated Modelling and SimulatiON) software environment. CRIMSON provides a powerful, customizable and user-friendly system for performing three-dimensional and reduced-order computational haemodynamics studies via a pipeline which involves: 1) segmenting vascular structures from medical images; 2) constructing analytic arterial and venous geometric models; 3) performing finite element mesh generation; 4) designing, and 5) applying boundary conditions; 6) running incompressible Navier-Stokes simulations of blood flow with fluid-structure interaction capabilities; and 7) post-processing and visualizing the results, including velocity, pressure and wall shear stress fields. A key aim of CRIMSON is to create a software environment that makes powerful computational haemodynamics tools accessible to a wide audience, including clinicians and students, both within our research laboratories and throughout the community. The overall philosophy is to leverage best-in-class open source standards for medical image processing, parallel flow computation, geometric solid modelling, data assimilation, and mesh generation. top_cited_works.title: Three-dimensional interactions between a finite-span synthetic jet and a crossflow
top_cited_works.abstract: A complementary experimental and numerical investigation was performed to study the three-dimensional flow structures and interactions of a finite-span synthetic jet in a crossflow at a chord-based Reynolds number of 100,000 and a 0° angle of attack. Six blowing ratios in the range of 0.2–1.2 were considered. Experiments were conducted on a finite wing with a cross-sectional profile of NACA 4421, where particle-image velocimetry data were collected at the centre jet. To complement the experiments, three-dimensional numerical simulations were performed, where the numerical set-up matched not only the physical parameters (e.g. free stream) but also the physical dimensions (e.g. orientation and location of the jet. For the low blowing ratio cases, spatial non-uniformities developed, due to the finite span of the slit, which led to the formation of small and organized secondary structures or a streak-like pattern in the mean flow. On the other hand, for the high blowing ratio range, turbulent vortical structures were dominant, leading to larger spanwise structures, with a larger spanwise wavelength. recent_works.title: Unstructured Mesh Tools for Fusion Energy System Design
recent_works.abstract: The execution of accurate simulations of fusion energy systems requires the appropriate representation of critical component geometries as well as the coupling of complex fusion physics codes with one another and with engineering analysis tools. This paper examines the challenges of creating simulation workflows that fully leverage existing fusion research codes while integrating them with commercial computer-aided engineering (CAE) software. Key areas addressed include: (a) the construction and meshing of analysis geometries taking full advantage of available geometric modeling and meshing technologies; (b) the effective coupling of fusion physics and engineering analysis codes; and (c) the support for simulation workflows that couple particle and continuum modeling methods.

recent_works.title: Hex-Dominant Boundary Layer Mesh Adaptation for Accurate Prediction of Surface Heat Flux in Hypersonic Problems
recent_works.abstract: We present a hex-dominant boundary layer mesh adaptation approach for accurate prediction of surface heat flux in hypersonic problems. We build upon our prior work on an automated workflow for in-memory parallel anisotropic mesh adaptation for hypersonic problems. Our workflow combines three simulation components to target such problems, namely, a hypersonic flow solver; a library for geometry and mesh modification/adaptation; and an adaptation controller. Our approach is component based, in which different simulation components are selected and integrated in a flexible and modular fashion. In this work, a novel hex-dominant boundary layer mesh adaptation approach is investigated, in which surface mesh adaptation is applied with a control on element topology by using hierarchical refinement/de-refinement of the unstructured quad-dominant surface mesh as well as the associated hex-dominant boundary layer elements in the surface-normal direction along the boundary layer thickness. This results in semi-structured hex-dominant boundary layer elements and retains the geometric flexibility due to the use of an unstructured quad-dominant surface mesh. Mesh Adaptation for Accurate Prediction of Surface Heat Flux in Hypersonic Problems
recent_works.abstract: In this paper, we present a mesh adaptation approach for accurate prediction of surface heat flux in hypersonic problems. We build upon our prior work on an automated workflow for in-memory parallel anisotropic mesh adaptation for hypersonic problems. Our workflow combines three simulation components to target such problems. Namely, a hypersonic flow solver; a library for geometry and mesh modification/adaptation; and an adaptation controller. Our approach is component based, in which different simulation components are combined and plugged in a flexible and modular fashion. This paper builds upon our previous work and focuses on accurate computation of the surface heat flux. In particular, we focus on three mesh-related aspects: i) mesh topology on walls including triangular and quad-dominant surface meshes, ii) finer mesh near the shock with high anisotropy, and iii) rapid mesh gradation in the upstream region of the shock. The utility of the current approach is shown by accurate prediction of surface heat flux on two hypersonic flow cases: a hemisphere case and a crew exploration vehicle case.
